section.x: North of the Limpopo: slave and ivory states, 1800 to 1880

Isaacman's chapter in UNESCO's volume VI opens against a simple story that nineteenth-century change came from outside. He shows Shona and Lunda state systems already in place, trading networks in iron, salt, cloth and grain, and recurring succession crises and secession. What was new in the nineteenth century, he argues, was not change but its speed. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

The old label 'subsistence-oriented' does not fit. Sena weavers sold cloth hundreds of kilometres away, Bisa traders dealt in iron through the eighteenth century, and the Chewa of Kasungu traded salt for Tumbuka hoes. The coast had been supplied with ivory, gold and copper from the interior in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, though on a small and irregular scale until the last two decades of the eighteenth century. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

Demand then rose from several directions: Brazil and Cuba, French planters on Bourbon (now Reunion) and the Mascarenes, Madagascar, and clove plantations on Zanzibar and Pemba. Annual exports from Quelimane to Brazil rose by 400 per cent between 1800 and 1835, which is five times the 1800 figure (our arithmetic), and Zanzibar's imports rose from 10000 a year in 1810 to at least 20000 in 1850. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

The carriers of the trade were African as well as coastal. Yao, Bisa and Chikunda merchants worked inland, Makua chiefs took over the supply to Mozambique Island by the mid-century, Nyamwezi traders reached eastern Lunda under Msiri, and Mambari traders came from Angola. By the middle of the century, Isaacman says, much of the region north of the Zambezi had become a labour reserve in which the main activity was 'producing' slaves. {{gha6-isaacman}} [CONTESTED]

After 1840 raiding and conquest replaced purchase. Chikunda traditions say they first bought criminals, outcasts and strangers and later used coercion. Conquest states followed: Massangano, Makanga and the Zumbo states on the Zambezi, and the Yao chiefs Mataka, Makanjila and Mponda in the Shire valley. In 1872 Arab and Swahili traders helped arrange the assassination of the Lunda king Kazembe Muonga Sunkutu and the choice of a more pliant successor. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

The effects were uneven. The Bemba, away from the main routes and not trade rivals, expanded between 1860 and 1880 and conquered most of north-eastern Zambia. The Chewa chief Mwase Kasungu supplied caravans and bought guns that helped him withstand Nguni attack. The Makua, by contrast, ended up raiding each other and enslaving their own people, and Isaacman says that most prazos were destroyed by 1830 as their holders began enslaving their own tenants. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

The Shona-dominated south was spared the worst. Population was thinner, the Shona states had gold and ivory to sell, and they could repel raids: the Mwenemutapa's army defeated a Portuguese force in 1807. After 1850 the British blockade of Lourenco Marques and Inhambane made the trade unprofitable, and within a decade the Gaza aristocracy stopped exporting captives, using them at home. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

As exports fell later in the century, captives became forced labour at home. Among the Lozi, Isaacman reports an estimate that a quarter of the population were slaves by the last quarter of the century. He argues that the slavery was changing in kind as it moved away from kin-based forms to chattel labour. {{gha6-isaacman}} [THIN EVIDENCE]

He also draws a heavy balance sheet: raids, famine, smallpox epidemics documented in Mozambique in 1834, 1836 and 1862, cholera and sleeping sickness. One report, from a British official in 1861, repeats an Arab's account of seventeen days' travel through ruined towns near Lake Nyasa. That is a report of a report, so use it as an impression and not a measurement. {{gha6-isaacman}} [THIN EVIDENCE]

His wider interpretation is a world-systems one: the region was 'incorporated' into a capitalist world economy and 'underdeveloped'. New crops and tools, he says, were insignificant beside the economic retardation. That is an argument, to set beside Ajayi and Wallerstein in Module 8. Test it against what you know of the Bemba and the Zulu. {{gha6-isaacman}} [CONTESTED]

section.title: Worked example: reading growth in the Zanzibar figures (our arithmetic)
steps: Isaacman says imports rose from 10000 a year in 1810 to at least 20000 in 1850.
That is a doubling in 40 years. The gain of 10000 over 40 years is an average of 250 more captives a year, each year.
The word 'at least' makes 20000 a floor, so the real gain could be larger. Isaacman cites Alpers for the figures, so they are secondary estimates.

section.x: Gaza, Ngoni and Kololo: kingdoms built from newcomers

Isaacman places the Nguni and Sotho movements of the 1820s onwards inside the longer story, citing new work by Bonner, Guy, Hedges and Slater that finds the roots of Nguni state-building in earlier chiefly consolidation. He sees three waves: the Gaza under Soshangane, the Ngoni under Zwangendaba, and the Kololo under Sebetwane. {{gha6-isaacman}} [CONTESTED]

Soshangane moved up to the Delagoa Bay region by 1821, defeated Zwangendaba in 1831, set his capital at Chaimaite and raided Manica, Quiteve and Barue, taking tribute from the prazeros at Sena and Tete. His core was ruled harshly: Tonga and Chopi youths were put into segregated age-regiments under Nguni officers, and Tonga and Chopi chiefs sometimes allied with the Portuguese. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

Zwangendaba started with about 300 people and trekked twenty years, giving the Rozwi their final blow, before settling at Mapupo. He adopted outsiders into Nguni families and age-regiments, so that an estimated 90 per cent of the Nguni at Mapupo in the 1840s were of foreign descent. After his death the state fragmented into the Mpezeni, Mbwela and other groups, and the Gwangara moved into Tanzania. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

The Kololo under Sebetwane reached the Lozi frontier around 1835 and conquered the kingdom within four years, helped by a leadership vacuum after Mulambwa's death and resentment among subject provinces. Sebetwane married into local families, made Kololo the national language and declared 'all are children of the king'. After he died in 1863, Sekeletu reversed that, shut out the Lozi, and in 1864 the Lozi rose and killed virtually all the Kololo men. {{gha6-isaacman}} [PROBABLE]

section.x: On the eve of the Scramble Isaacman judges most societies weaker, apart from the Bemba at their height before the death of Mwamba III, a stronger Lozi kingdom under Lewanika and a revived Mwenemutapa state. He adds that many subjects of the conquest states saw Europeans as liberators, which hampered joint resistance. That judgement needs testing against local sources. {{gha6-isaacman}} [CONTESTED]
Pick two groups from the table and write what a Lozi, a Tonga and a Portuguese official would each have said about them. Mark which statements come from the chapter and which are your guesses.

checks.q: A website says: 'The slave trade only reached Central Africa when Europeans arrived in the 1800s, and Africans were just victims.' What does Isaacman's chapter suggest is wrong with that sentence?
o: Local traders and rulers shaped the trade
The buyers, because he says all captives went to the Americas and none to Zanzibar
The place, because he says the slave trade never touched the Zambezi basin
Nothing, because he says Africans played no part and only coastal powers acted
The date, because he says the trade began only with the Nguni invasions of 1820
checks.w: He shows trading networks before 1800 and Yao, Bisa, Chikunda, Makua and Swahili merchants and conquest states as active agents, while also arguing the region became dependent on outside markets. {{gha6-isaacman}}

checks.q: An essay quotes a British official of 1861 who said an Arab had travelled seventeen days through a country 'covered with ruined towns and villages'. How should a careful student use that quotation?
o: As a number to put in a table, after turning seventeen days into kilometres
As proof of exact depopulation, because the official saw the towns himself
As a second-hand impression, not a measurement
As proof that the Arab invented the account, because traders always lied
As the only needed evidence, because one official outweighs all other sources
checks.w: The chapter's report is the official passing on what the Arab told him, so it is evidence of what was said, tagged [THIN EVIDENCE]. {{gha6-isaacman}}

checks.q: A student says: 'The Kololo kept ruling the Lozi until the British came, because the Kololo were the stronger army.' Which reply does Isaacman's account support?
o: That is wrong, because the Lozi were conquered by the Gaza in 1831
That is right, because the Kololo fell only in 1890 to a British column
That is wrong, because the Kololo had never ruled the Lozi at all
That is right, because Sebetwane lived until 1864 and kept the Lozi down
The Lozi rose in 1864 after Sekeletu's policy
checks.w: He says Sekeletu shut the Lozi out of government, they rebelled in 1864 and killed virtually all the Kololo men, though the Kololo language and some institutions stayed. {{gha6-isaacman}}
